DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay two-storey former Superintendent�s house, c. 1890, with pair of canted bay windows flanking gabled projecting porch.  Timber panelled door and fanlight set into a four-centred arch with yellow brick keystone. Red brick walls with yellow brick bands and decorative tiled panel.  Segmental- and flat-arched window openings with stone sills and brick aprons, housing uPVC windows.  Pitched slate roofs with cresting, red brick chimney stacks, timber barge boards and tile-hung gables.  Stone steps to entrance.  Now in use as nurses' training centre.
APPRAISAL: This is a fine, rich example of Victorian design, craftsmanship and detailing employed on a building of significance to the hospital, which still contributes positively to its environment.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached single-storey outbuilding, c. 1790, on a L-plan.  Fa�ade to north east is rendered, ruled and lined, with four-centre arched doorway having double-leaf sheet metal door and drip moulding over.  Stepped crenellated parapet with corner finials and blind cross motif below drip moulding.  Rubble stone walls, roughcast rendered facing yard.  Pitched slate roofs.  Several lean-to structures attached.
APPRAISAL: The outbuilding is small and of simple design with a striking fa�ade facing the main house.  It retains substantial original fabric, and still serves the grounds in which it is sited.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: End-of-terrace two-bay single-storey with dormer attic former almshouse, built 1879, now in use as a private house.  Coursed limestone construction with beige brick dressings to openings.  Timber sash windows with granite sills.  Single-storey bay to north with a lean-to roof housing a replacement timber tongue and groove door.  Hipped slate roof with shared beige brick chimney stack.  Limestone rubble wall with rubble coping to street front.
APPRAISAL: This terrace of four former almshouses is set in the very historic Tower Road and blends in beautifully with St. John�s Church to the north and the former National School building to the south.  It was constructed in 1879 in memory of Reverend David John Reade and this historic connection is set in a smooth limestone plaque in the centre of the houses.  They have been excellently maintained with the original style of fenestration and  matching timber panelled doors.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

Timber sash windows with granite sills.  Replacement timber tongue and groove door with slate porch hood supported by a timber frame above.  Inset commemorative plaque below dormer sills.  Pitched slate roof with shared beige brick chimney stacks.  Limestone rubble wall with rubble coping to street front.

Now in use as a private house.  Coursed limestone construction with beige brick dressings to openings.  Timber sash windows with granite sills.  Replacement timber tongue and groove door. DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay two-storey former house, c.1840, now in use as a variety of commercial premises.  Smooth rendered walls.  Timber sash windows with stone sills to first floor.  Pair of plain late twentieth-century shopfronts to partly tiled ground floor flanking central doorway.  Pitched slate roof with chimney stack and raised coping to each gable.  Two-storey flat-roofed extension to rere.
APPRAISAL: Though much altered externally, this building possesses a presence not wholly diminished by the surface changes.  Its street front situation makes it highly likely that the building has a long history of commercial usage which continues today.  A valuable historic element in this commercial part of the village.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron water pump, c.1880, set in a small concrete base, with fluted cap and slender handle.
APPRAISAL: A fine example of an increasingly rare feature in village centres, this water pump adds character and a sense of history to this busy junction.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached two-bay two-storey section of detached five-bay building, c.1820, now in use as a commercial premises. Roughcast rendered walls to first floor with timber sash windows having stone sills.  Smooth rendered to ground floor with altered openings, including former round-headed doorway now containing window.  Glazed aluminium door in flat-roofed single-storey extension to side.  Hipped slate roof with projecting eaves and red brick chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: The formerly detached five-bay building, of which this is a section, is a handsome, substantial edifice on this village street.  Its retention of its original proportions and some materials adds greatly to the character of this commercial area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached three-bay two-storey section of detached five-bay building, c.1820, also in use as a shop.  Roughcast rendered walls to first floor, smooth rendered to ground floor.  Timber sash windows with stone sills.  Timber panelled door with timber surround and plain fanlight.  Simple modern shopfront to eastern bay.  Hipped slate roof with projecting eaves and smooth rendered chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: The formerly detached five-bay building, of which this is a section, is a handsome, substantial edifice on this village street.  Its retention of its original proportions and some materials adds greatly to the character of this commercial area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached multiple-bay single-storey former gate lodge, c.1850, on an L-shaped plan.  Now in use as a detached house.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Timber casement windows with stone sills.  Hipped slate roof to front, pitched to rere, with smooth rendered chimney stacks.  Flat-roofed porch extension containing entrance to re-entrant corner.  Set inside modern gateway having pair of carved limestone plaques.
APPRAISAL: A simple former gate lodge with many original materials, enhancing the charm which it contributes to this road and to the college entrance.  Visually prominent when viewed from the village to the north.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Mill race, c.1850, with associated concrete weir, walls and sluice on the Cammock River.  Mill race no longer functional, and now forms pond.
APPRAISAL: This mill race is valuable evidence of the former land use in this part of Clondalkin.  Though now disused, it remains important as a feature of the nearby parkland and as a wildlife habitat.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron former water pump, dated 1860.  Now capped with concrete and no longer functional.
APPRAISAL: A simple, decorative former water pump which, though no longer operational, adds variety and visual interest to this stretch of Tower Road.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay two-storey house, c.1840.  Roughcast rendered walls with smooth rendered base course.  Timber sash windows with stone sills and glazed timber panelled door.  Pitched slate roof with roughcast rendered chimney stacks to gables.  Extension to rere.
APPRAISAL: A modest detached house, retaining its original proportions and some materials, which adds variety to the mostly twentieth-century streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached two-bay single-storey house, c.1910, with door to side.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Aluminium casement windows.  Hipped slate roof with brick chimney stack.  Single-storey extension to rere.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of sixteen semi-detached houses built in a row.  Most houses have undergone alterations and extensions, showing how these modest structures have been adapted as the needs of the occupants changed.  This house retains its original proportions and some materials.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached two-bay single-storey house, c.1910, with door to side.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Replacement timber casement windows.  Timber panelled door.  Hipped slate roof with brick chimney stack.  Large single-storey red brick extension with pyramidal roof to rere.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of sixteen semi-detached houses built in a row.  Most houses have undergone alterations and extensions, showing how these modest structures have been adapted as the needs of the occupants changed.  This house retains its original proportions and some materials.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Timber sash windows.  Timber door.  Pitched slate roof with brick chimney stacks.  Iron bar gate to street.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of sixteen semi-detached houses built in a row.  Most houses have undergone alterations and extensions, showing how these modest structures have been adapted as the needs of the occupants changed.  This house is one of the few to retain its original proportions and materials throughout, showing the original appearance of some of the group.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910.  Random stone-clad walls.  Replacement timber casement windows.  Replacement timber door set into glazed projecting porch.  Pitched slate roof with brick chimney stacks.  Single-storey extension to east side of house with hipped roof.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of sixteen semi-detached houses built in a row.  Most houses have undergone alterations and extensions, showing how these modest structures have been adapted as the needs of the occupants changed.  This house retainssome of its original proportions.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron former water pump, dated 1860, now disused.  Fluted shaft with manufacturer's name to front.
APPRAISAL: An attractive piece of street furniture which enhances this quiet residential road of buildings which post-date this feature.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached three-bay single-storey house, c.1900, with projecting gabled brick porch.  Brick walls with painted brick quoins and opening surrounds.  Timber sash windows with granite lintels and sills.  Replacement glazed timber door with granite lintel and semi-circular three pane fixed overlight.  Pitched slate roof with terracotta ridge tiles and a central brick chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of six semi-detached houses of simple proportions and robust detailing.  Most houses have been refurbished to some degree, showing a variety of examples of twentieth-century tastes.  This is the only house to remain substantially intact, showing how the others once would have looked.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached three-bay single-storey house, c.1900, with projecting gabled brick porch.  Brick walls with painted brick quoins and opening surrounds.  uPVC casement windows with granite lintels and sills.  Glazed aluminium door with granite lintel and plain semi-circular fixed overlight.  Pitched slate roof with terracotta ridge tiles and a central brick chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of six semi-detached houses of simple proportions and robust detailing.  Most houses have been refurbished to some degree, showing a variety of examples of twentieth-century tastes.  This house retains its original proportions and some materials.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached three-bay single-storey house, c.1900, with projecting gabled porch.  Imitation stone-clad front wall, smooth rendered to sides.  Aluminium casement windows with granite lintels and sills.  Replacement glazed timber door with granite lintel and semi-circular three pane fixed overlight.  Pitched slate roof with terracotta ridge tiles and a central brick chimney stack.  Extension to rere.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of six semi-detached houses of simple proportions and robust detailing.  Most houses have been refurbished to some degree, showing a variety of examples of twentieth-century tastes.  This house retains its original proportions and some materials.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

Yellow brick walls with red brick quoins and opening surrounds.  uPVC casement windows with granite lintels and sills.  Granite lintel and semi-circular three pane fixed overlight to porch.  Pitched artificial slate roof with central brick chimney stack.  Iron bar gate to street.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of six semi-detached houses of simple proportions and robust detailing.  Most houses have been refurbished to some degree, showing a variety of examples of twentieth-century tastes.  This house retains its original proportions and some materials.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached three-bay single-storey house, c.1900, with projecting gabled brick porch.  Painted brick walls with contrasting painted brick quoins and opening surrounds.  uPVC casement windows with granite lintels and sills.  uPVC door with granite lintel and semi-circular three pane fixed overlight.  Pitched artificial slate roof with central brick chimney stack.  Iron bar gate to street.
APPRAISAL: One of a group of six semi-detached houses of simple proportions and robust detailing.  Most houses have been refurbished to some degree, showing a variety of examples of twentieth-century tastes.  This house retains its original proportions and some materials.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached five-bay two-storey former stables, c.1780, now in use as an office.  Limestone rubble walls.  Elliptical-headed carriage arch to centre bay with timber sash window and round-headed doorway flanking to each side.  Timber hinged windows to first floor round openings with cut stone surrounds.  uPVC casement windows to roughcast rere elevation.  Pitched concrete tile roof with bellcote to the east gable.  Smaller single-storey sheds to the south.
APPRAISAL: This former outbuilding, which retains its original proportions, has been respectfully restored and is a valuable asset to the overall complex of buildings at Belgard Castle. It complements the historic fabric whilst still functioning in the modern context.  The series of openings to the ground floor is a particularly attractive feature.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached five-bay single-storey house, c.1860.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Timber casement windows and timber door.  Pitched slate roof with red brick chimney stack.  Single-storey extension to west.  Iron bar gate set into partially rendered rubble gate piers.
APPRAISAL: A modest house retaining its original proportions.  Its presence on this road is a valuable reminder of the former rural character of the area, which is now becoming increasingly suburbanised.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Group of five terraced three-bay single-storey former houses, c.1840, now in use as park offices.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Replacement timber casement windows with stone sills.  Replacement timber panelled doors.  Pitched slate roof with both brick and smooth rendered chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: These former houses are part of a group of outbuildings associated with the past Corkagh House. These simple structures have a practical, modest character and  are an important reminder of the history of the surrounding parkland and the heritage of the Clondalkin area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached multiple-bay two-storey former stables, c.1800, on an L-shaped plan, now in use as park outbuildings.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Multiple shuttered doorways to ground floor.  Rectangular openings with stone sills and elliptical openings with red brick dressings to first floor.  Round-headed archway with dressed voussoir stones.  Half-hipped slate roofs.  Dilapidated single-storey accommodation block to north-west. Semi-circular limestone rubble boundary wall and gate piers associated with stables to north west.
APPRAISAL: The stable block is part of a group of outbuildings associated with the former Corkagh House. The design of the modest structure is enlivened by the use of brick dressed oval openings and the grand archway. The stable block is an important reminder of the history of the surrounding parkland and the heritage of the Clondalkin area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Section of watercourse, c.1810, with single arch rubble stone bridge having cut stone voussoirs to each end.  Canalised limestone-lined stream between bridges, with shallow inclined bank to south side having squared limestone kerbing.
APPRAISAL: This feature is an ancillary structure associated with the former Corkagh House.  Retaining much original fabric, it is an unusual feature combining practicality and elegance.  A feature such as this is an important reminder of the history of the surrounding parkland and the heritage of the Clondalkin area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron pillar post box, c.1950, with 'Post Office' lettering and manufacturer's name to base.
APPRAISAL: A simple mid twentieth-century post box which adds a welcome historic note to this corner shopfront.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Entrance gateway, c.1880, comprising monolithic granite gate piers with carved caps, outer flanking piers, cast- and wrought-iron gates and railings, and squared limestone quadrant walls with blocked pedestrian gateway.
APPRAISAL: An attractive entrance ensemble of simple, robust design, which enhances this narrow laneway and the approach to the modern house beyond.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Decorative wrought-iron gates and square rubble piers, c.1870.  Pedestrian gates to either side, carriage lamps to piers.  Gates incorporate spiral twists and scrolled ornament.
APPRAISAL: These unusually elaborate modern gates update the traditional Irish country house entrance. They contrast in time and style with the outer set of original gates which led to the now-demolished older house.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron vent pipe, date 1912, with bulbous base.  'S.D.  R.D.C.' logo and manufacturer's name plate to north side.
APPRAISAL: A simple piece of historic street furniture with attractive detailing which adds character to the streetscape and enhances the setting of the graveyard gateway.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Enclosed graveyard, c. 1720, containing ruins of former church, c.1600, comprising west gable with bellcote and chancel arch in section of wall.  Segmental archway to entrance with crenellated parapet and wrought-iron gate, set in rubble stone boundary wall.  Graveyard contains collection of headstones and tombs dating from the early eighteenth century onwards and still in use.
APPRAISAL: This site has a rich history, having changed from Roman Catholic to Church of Ireland in the eighteenth century.  Contains medieval fabric and a number of finely carved gravestones, including those of the Shaw and Yelverton families.  Robust entrance adds interest to this northern end of Rathfarnham village.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: End-of-terrace corner-sited three-bay single-storey school house with dormer attic, c.1820, with central gabled entrance breakfront.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Chamfered stone reveals to windows.  Replacement timber casement windows with drip mouldings.  Timber tongue and groove door in four-centred archway.  Pair of blind recessed panels to attic of outer bays with semi-circular coping above.  Pitched slate roof with cut stone gable copings and rendered chimney stack to rere.  Adjoins former school to rere.
APPRAISAL: Located at the corner of the churchyard, this attractive school house with much character visually aids the transition from the southern two-storey commercial row to the religious group to the north, with which it is still associated.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached circular-plan two-storey former dovecote, c.1770.  Roughcast rendered walls with blind quatrefoil and pointed openings to exterior.  Brick to interior with regularly spaced nesting boxes.  Timber tongue and groove door in pointed opening.  Access hatch to upper section.  Unroofed.
APPRAISAL: A bold, simple structural volume, retaining its original form and many materials.  Originally within the curtilage of Rathfarnham Castle, it is a valuable document of the extent and activities of this demesne.  Now stands as a strong and, to contemporary eyes, almost sculptural feature within a domestic garden.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: End-of-terrace three-bay single-storey house, c.1900. Smooth rendered walls.  Glazed aluminium door and aluminium casement windows in enlarged openings. Pitched slate roof with rendered chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: A modest terraced house which, though altered, retains its original massing and, as part of this small close-built group, enhances the approach to the river walkway.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Terraced three-bay single-storey house, c.1900.  Rendered, ruled and lined walls.  Glazed uPVC door and uPVC windows.  Pitched slate roof with rendered chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: A modest terraced house which, though refurbished, retains its original proportions and, as part of this small close-built group, enhances the approach to the river walkway.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: End-of-terrace three-bay single-storey house, c.1900. Smooth rendered walls.  Timber door and uPVC casement windows.  Pitched slate roof with rendered chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: A modest terraced house which, though refurbished, retains its original proportions and, as part of this small close-built group, enhances the approach to the river walkway.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: End-of-terrace single-bay two-storey house, c. 1890, with later projecting porch to side.  Rendered, ruled and lined walls.  uPVC glazed doors, one in porch to side.  uPVC casement windows. M-profile slate roof with rendered chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: A modest terraced house which, though refurbished, retains its original proportions and which contrasts well in scale with the modern road level.  Enhances the approach to the river walkway as part of this small, close-built group.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Terraced single-bay two-storey house, c.1890.  Rendered, ruled and lined walls.  Timber glazed door and uPVC casement windows.  M-profile slate roof with rendered chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: A modest terraced house which, though refurbished, retains its original proportions and which contrasts well in scale with the modern road level.  Enhances the approach to the river walkway as part of this small, close-built group.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Terraced single-bay two-storey house, c.1890.  Rendered, ruled and lined walls.  Timber glazed door and timber casement windows.  M-profile slate roof with rendered chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: A modest terraced house which, though refurbished, retains its original proportions and which contrasts well in scale with the modern road level.  Enhances the approach to the river walkway as part of this small, close-built group.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: End-of-terrace single-bay two-storey house, c.1890.  Rendered, ruled and lined walls.  Glazed uPVC door and uPVC casement windows.  Pitched slate roof with rendered chimney stack.  Original rear half now demolished.
APPRAISAL: A modest terraced house which, though altered and reduced in size, retains its original proportions and which contrasts well in scale with the modern road level.  Enhances the approach to the river walkway as part of this small, close-built group.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Formerly semi-detached four-bay single-storey school house, c.1820.  Roughcast rendered walls with cut stone dressings.  Chamfered stone reveals to openings.  Leaded timber casement windows.  Timber tongue and groove door in four-centred archway to gabled breakfront.  Pitched slate roof with cut stone coping to breakfront gable.
APPRAISAL: An attractive school house, retaining many original features and finishes.  Built alongside the former Sexton's House and in the same style, the school adds character to this religious group at the northern end of Rathfarnham village.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Two stage weir in the River Dodder, c.1800, originally supplying water for a mill stream.  First tier constructed of cobbled slabs, cobbles and cement, has a curving profile over c.10 metres with a drop of c. 3 metres.  Second tier constructed of slabs, has a length of c.5 metres and vertical drop of c. 2 metres.  Overall width of c.25 metres leads to millstream, sluice and overflow on north bank. Substantial revetment walls downstream.
APPRAISAL: Though now obsloete, this weir today provides a stimulating sight on the River Dodder, and is a recreational fishing location. It is an important remnant of the industrial age in this area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron hydrant, c.1860, with fluted shaft, decorative lion's head motif and manufacturer's mark.  Painted bright green.
APPRAISAL: Prominently set at side of road, this cast-iron hydrant is an attractive piece of street furniture enhancing the streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached five-bay two-storey house, c.1820.  Coursed rubble limestone walls.  Rendered, ruled and lined east gable.  Timber casement windows with brick dressings.  Glazed timber panelled door with gabled hood.  Pitched slate roof with smooth rendered chimney stack.  Single-storey extension to rere.
APPRAISAL: This handsome, balanced house, retaining much original fabric, is an imposing element in the streetscape due to its street front location and larger than usual size.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached five-bay single-storey house comprising original three-bay house, c.1930, and two-bay extension to south, c.1960.  Roughcast rendered walls with smooth rendered base course.  Timber sash windows to pair of canted bay windows flanking replacement glazed timber door approached by flight of stone steps.  Timber casement windows to extension.  Hipped slate roof with smooth rendered chimney stacks.  Limestone rubble walls to road with wrought-iron gate.
APPRAISAL: An attractive small house of simple design set in quiet rural atmosphere, enhanced by the surrounding trees and the simple iron entrance gate.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached two-bay two-storey outbuilding, c.1890.  Roughcast rendering over possible mud wall construction.  Metal casement windows and sheet metal rolling doorway.  External stair to north-east elevation.  Replacement corrugated metal roof.
APPRAISAL: An outbuilding of functional design, possibly constructed using mud walls, a technique not often surviving in this area.  Although simple in character, the structure is a valuable addition to the rural environment.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached five-bay single-storey farmhouse, c.1860.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Timber casement windows.  Glazed timber door in gable-ended projecting porch.  Pitched slate roof with smooth rendered chimney stacks.  Cylindrical squared stone gate piers with iron bar half-moon gate to north side of house.  Modern outbuildings to north and east.
APPRAISAL: A simple, unpretentious house, retaining its original proportions, which is part of a group of farm buildings.  The cylindrical gate piers and iron gate, both peculiar to this area, and the unusual porch, enhance the vernacular quality of this group.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1915.  Smooth rendered walls.  Timber casement windows.  Modern gable-fronted projecting porch with timber door to side.  Pitched diagonally-tiled roof with two rendered chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: This cottage is beautifully set in a rural location and retains some original fabric.  It is part of a group of four properties in the area which share the unusual characteristic of the diagonally-tiled roof.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1915.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Timber sash windows.  Projecting lean-to porch with glazed timber door.  Pitched diagonally-tiled roof with two rendered chimney stacks.  Roughcast rendered boundary wall.  Rubble stone outbuildings to rere.
APPRAISAL: This cottage is beautifully set in a rural location and retains substantial original fabric.  It is part of a group of four properties in the area which share the unusual characteristic of the diagonally-tiled roof.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached five-bay single-storey house, c.1915, with the original building four bays to the east.  Smooth rendered walls.  uPVC casement windows.  Projecting lean-to porch with timber panelled door.  Pitched diagonally-tiled roof with two rendered chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: This cottage is beautifully set in a rural location and retains much original fabric.  It is part of a group of four properties in the area which share the unusual characteristic of the diagonally-tiled roof.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay single-storey house, c.1820.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Timber tongue and groove door.  Timber sash windows.  Pitched slate roof with brick chimney stack.  Single-bay extension to north with corrugated roof.
APPRAISAL: A well-maintained structure with simple design, retaining much original fabric.  Due to its alternative alignment perpendicular to the road, the house stands out among the surrounding modern houses.  The structure's pleasing character is a valuable addition to the village.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron pillar post box, c.1960, with �P & T� mark to roadside.
APPRAISAL: A fine mid twentieth-century traditional style post box with crisp detailing, which enhances the streetscape and the busy filling station behind.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron hydrant, c.1860.  Fluted shaft and domed cap with acorn finial.  Lion�s head to street front above maker's mark.
APPRAISAL: This cast-iron hydrant is an important feature in the village fabric and, due to their increasing rarity, is a very valuable element of the streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached five-bay single-storey farmhouse, c.1820.  Timber casement windows.  Timber tongue and groove door.  Smooth rendered walls.  Pitched slate roof with red brick chimney stacks.  Cast-iron gate to road.  Multiple outbuildings of painted stone rubble construction and corrugated-iron roofs to north-east and south-east.
APPRAISAL: This farmhouse and its associated farm buildings, due to the retention of much original fabric and a harmonious, distinctive colour scheme, form a most attractive group along this country road.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay two-storey house, c.1700.  Replacement timber casement windows with smooth rendered surrounds.  Smooth rendered walls.  Half-hipped thatched roof with brick chimney stack.  Entrance incorporated into gabled porch extension.  Three-bay two-storey extension to west in similar style.  Three-bay two-storey more recent extension to south.
APPRAISAL: This house is one of the oldest surviving structures in Rathccoole and, though quite altered and refurbished, remains a valuable element of the local history, long in use as a public house.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron hydrant, c.1860.  Fluted shaft with domed cap having acorn finial.  Decorative lion's head motif above maker's mark.  Painted black and gold.
APPRAISAL: Prominently set at side of road, this cast-iron hydrant is a welcome addition to the streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay single-storey national school teacher's house with dormer attic, c.1870.  uPVC casement windows.  Roughcast rendered walls with smooth rendered base course.  Red brick dressings to openings.  Shallow projecting brick porch with timber panelled door.  Single central gable with two half dormers.  Pitched slate roof with central red brick chimney stack.  Limestone rubble wall to west, roughcast rendered wall and gate piers to street front.
APPRAISAL: This house is located to the immediate east of Rathcoole National School and shares many of its architectural features such as the brick dressings and the gables to the front elevations. The general character of this house is quite pleasant and, set back slightly from the road, it retains its former importance within the streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron pillar post box, c.1990, with 'An Post' logo to roadside.
APPRAISAL: This modern, traditional-style cast-iron post box shows continuity of form, adding greater character to its modern street setting.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached eight-bay two-storey inn, c.1785.  Eastern three bays a later extension.  Smooth rendered ground floor and roughcast rendered first floor walls with raised quoins.  Replacement timber casement windows and doors throughout.  Thatched roof with gable end chimney to west and small, possibly original, rendered chimney stack to east.  Modern extensions to rere.
APPRAISAL: A handsome vernacular inn which, due to its substantial size, well maintained fa�ade and large thatched roof, is a prominent element in the streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Terraced three-bay two-storey house c.1870, now divided into multiple commercial properties.  Roughcast rendered walls.  uPVC casement windows to first floor. Timber shop front with fascia board and console brackets inserted into western ground floor bay, c.1910.  uPVC shop front inserted into eastern ground floor bay.  Central timber door.  Pitched slate roof with parapet and smooth rendered chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: A modest village building with pleasing symmetry which, despite refurbishment, retains much of the fabric of its fine timber shopfront indicating a history of commercial use.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached three-bay two-storey house, c.1840.  uPVC casement windows, one in enlarged opening.  uPVC door.  Roughcast rendered walls with smooth rendered base course.  Hipped artificial slate roof with central smooth rendered chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: This house forms a strong group with its eastern neighbour, retaining much original fabric and showing the former character of the village street, with street-fronted dwellings lacking any parallel commercial usage.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay two-storey house, c.1840, now unoccupied.  Smooth rendered walls.  Boarded-up windows and doors.  Hipped slate roof with brick chimney stack.  Ruined outbuilding to north.
APPRAISAL: This house forms a strong group with its western neighbour, retaining much original fabric and showing the former character of the village street, with street-fronted dwellings lacking any parallel commercial usage.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached three-bay single-storey house, c.1820.  Metal casement windows.  Timber door.  Smooth rendered walls with smooth rendered base course.  Pitched slate roof with red brick chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: Though partly refurbished, this house adds welcome variety to the streetscape due to its modest size and continuity of use as a dwelling.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached three-bay single-storey house, c.1820.  Painted rubble walls with smooth rendered base course.  Boarded-up windows and doors.  Pitched slate roof with smooth rendered chimney stack.  Rubble wall to north.
APPRAISAL: Though in poor condition, the retention of its original proportions and many materials makes this house an important reminder of how the streetscape of Rathcoole has changed with time.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached five-bay two-storey house, c.1820.  Roughcast rendered walls with smooth rendered base course and quoins.  Timber sash windows.  Large timber panelled door with brass fittings and radial fanlight set in a moulded door surround.  Pitched slate roof with chimney stacks to each gable end, smooth rendered over red brick.  Two-bay single-storey wing to east of the same style, with a hipped slate roof.  Flat-roofed extension to west, c.1977.
APPRAISAL: This beautiful and well-maintained house retains all of its qualities and proportions, and an air of classical dignity due to its set back position.  Provides variety to, and visually enhances, the village streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron vent pipe, c.1880, with fluted base, slender shaft and crown cap, located to road side.
APPRAISAL: Prominently set at side of road, this cast-iron vent pipe adds variety to the streetscape.  An increasingly rare element of the suburban fabric, particularly in such an intact state.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron hydrant, c.1860.  Fluted shaft and domed cap.  Decorative lion's head motif above make's mark.  Painted green.
APPRAISAL: Prominently set at side of road, this standard type cast-iron hydrant is a pleasing addition to the streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron pillar post box, c.1960, with �P & T� mark to door.
APPRAISAL: A fine mid twentieth-century traditional-style cast-iron post box which blends well into its urban setting, adding greater character to the modern streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Former terrace of four two-bay two-storey houses, c.1880, now amalgamated.  Roughcast rendered walls with smooth rendered base course.  uPVC casement windows.  Timber doors.   Pitched slate roof with both brick and smooth rendered chimney stacks.  Extension to south-west elevation.
APPRAISAL: Though refurbished, this building is a valuable element of the village fabric.  The original proportions of the terraced houses have been retained demonstrating, in the change of use, a fine example of an evolution typical of many village and urban buildings.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Enclosed graveyard, established c.1880, set on an area of land sloping down to the north-west with a limestone rubble boundary wall having rubble coping.  Main entrance is to the south-east through a round-headed archway with limestone voussoirs and triangular pediment, with cast-iron cross finial above.  Gravestones date from 1890s to the present day.
APPRAISAL: This graveyard ,which contains many finely carved headstones and has a handsome entrance gate, has been in use since the 1890s, making it a very important social and religious focus of the people of Saggart.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay two-storey house, c.1880.  Beige brick walls with red brick quoins and timber cornice.  Roughcast rendering to sides.  Timber sash windows with stone sills and red brick dressings.  Timber panelled door with segmental-headed glazed timber surround and red brick dressings.  Hipped slate roof with perforated cresting and red brick chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: This modest house is a fine example of Victorian architecture, with a simple, attractive entrance and a skilful use of materials with the contrasting brickwork. The house is a valuable part of the village due to its strong contribution to the streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Single arch road bridge over river, c.1820.  Round-headed arch with dressed voussoir stones. Limestone rubble construction and parapets.
APPRAISAL: A simple bridge with an almost vernacular character, framed by local fields and vegetation.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Former mill pond, c.1780.  Buttressed limestone revetment wall and covered channel to west.  Elevated above road level.
APPRAISAL: A picturesque body of water and valuable habitat for local wildlife, this former mill pond is a strong reminder of the industrial heritage of the Saggart area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron pillar post box, c.1980, with circular projection to base.  Located next to roadside.
APPRAISAL: This late twentieth-century traditional style cast-iron post box blends well into its urban setting, adding greater character to the street.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay single-storey house, c.1840.  Smooth rendered walls with timber casement windows.  Central projecting flat-roofed porch.  M-profile slate roof with rendered chimney stack to southernmost gable end.  Low concrete wall to street front.
APPRAISAL: This small detached house still retains its original proportions and is discreetly set with the main entrance facing away from the road, adding character to this largely modern streetscape.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Monolithic square granite milestone, c.1800, with inscriptions to south and east faces.  Set into tarmac footpath.
APPRAISAL: This rugged granite pillar adds a strong character to the street, and is a reminder of the former prominence of the Old Naas road on which it stands, particularly in association with the nearby coaching inn.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached multiple-bay single-storey former house, c.1800, now derelict.  Rubble stone walls with possible mud wall construction also.  Variety of timber panelled doors and openings, quite ruinous.  Pitched corrugated-iron roof with roughcast rendered central chimney stack.  Another smaller chimney stack to the east gable.
APPRAISAL: This simple vernacular dwelling, though in poor condition, retains many materials of note, particularly its partial mud walls, a construction technique which rarely survives in this area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay two-storey house, c.1890.  Red brick walls with raised brick quoins.  Timber sash windows with stone sills.  Full-width glazed uPVC porch to altered ground floor.  Hipped slate roof with perforated cresting and red brick chimney stacks.  Shallow coursed rubble stone wall and gate piers to road.
APPRAISAL: A handsome, finely-detailed house, substantially intact and little compromised by the porch extension.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910.  uPVC windows with granite lintels.  Repointed granite rubble walls with painted brick dressings to openings.  Advanced gable-fronted porch with replacement timber panelled door.  Hipped slate roof with central red brick chimney stack.
APPRAISAL: One of a pair of semi-detached houses showing the quality of early twentieth-century local authority design.  This modest house retains some original fabric and its original proportions.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910, with advanced two-bay extension to east.  uPVC windows.  Roughcast rendered walls with smooth rendered base course.  Modern projecting gable-fronted porch with uPVC door.  Pitched tiled roof with central and shared beige brick chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: This house, though altered, retains some of its original proportions, and is an integral part of this group of modest early twentieth-century local authority houses set along a crescent.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910, with advanced two-bay extension to west.  uPVC windows.  Roughcast rendered walls with smooth rendered base course.   Original doorway blocked, uPVC door inserted to former window opening, and bay window added.  Pitched tiled roof with central and shared beige brick chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: This house, though altered, retains some of its original proportions, and is an integral part of this group of modest early twentieth-century local authority houses set along a crescent.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910. Timber sash windows.  Roughcast rendered walls with a smooth rendered base course.  Replacement timber panelled door with shallow projecting concrete surround.  Pitched tiled roof with central and shared beige brick chimney stacks.  Simple iron railings and gate to street.
APPRAISAL: This modest single-storey house is substantially intact, notably retaining its original windows, porch, gates and railings, and is an integral part of this group of early twentieth-century local authority houses set along a crescent, showing how its neighbours would have originally appeared.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910.  uPVC windows.  Roughcast rendered walls with a smooth rendered base course.  Glazed timber tongue and groove door in shallow projecting concrete surround.  Pitched tiled roof with central and shared beige brick chimney stacks.  Simple iron railings and gate to street.
APPRAISAL: This house, though partly refurbished, retains its original proportions and some features, including gates, railings and porch, and is an integral part of this group of modest early twentieth-century local authority houses set along a crescent.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910.  Replacement timber casement windows.  Roughcast rendered walls with a smooth rendered base course.  Timber tongue and groove door with shallow projecting concrete surround.  Pitched tiled roof with central and shared beige brick chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: This house, though refurbished, retains its original proportions, and is an integral part of this group of modest early twentieth-century local authority houses set along a crescent.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1910.  Replacement timber casement windows.  Roughcast rendered walls with a smooth rendered base course.  Glazed timber door with shallow projecting concrete surround.  Pitched tiled roof with central and shared beige brick chimney stacks.
APPRAISAL: This house, though partly refurbished, retains its original proportions and some materials, and is an integral part of this group of modest early twentieth-century local authority houses set along a crescent.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron pillar post box, c.1980, located to roadside.
APPRAISAL: This traditional-style cast-iron post box blends well into its urban setting, adding greater character to the street.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Pair of semi-detached single-storey with attic houses, c. 1825.  Roughcast walls with quoins.  Two segmental-headed door openings with drip moulding above each.  Square-headed window openings with stone sills and timber sash windows. Two small sash windows in gables of attic storey, some sash windows remaining to rere.  Pitched slate roof with central attic dormer window, perforated crested terracotta ridge tiles and four brick chimney stacks.  Projecting timber-bracketed  eaves. Shared extension to rere.  Large flat-roofed extension to rere of right-hand house.
APPRAISAL: The arrangement of a symmetrical fa�ade with single attic dormer means unequal internal division; an unusual type.  Retains many original features, and adds character to the setting of the nearby church.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Weir set perpendicular in River Dodder, c. 1875.  Approximately fifteen metres long set in four main stages from weir pool down to river, with an approximate drop of ten metres. Most stages built of concrete with large included pebbles.
APPRAISAL: This weir provides a dynamic aspect to the river readily observed from the bridge and playing fields. As little else remains in this area relating to the former mills and lades, the weir is a strong reminder of the former scale of works.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Terraced two-bay two-storey house on corner site, c.1820.  uPVC casement windows in roughcast walls with parapet wall to eaves and cornice to street.  Glazed timber door forming main entrance to rear. Pitched slate roof with rendered chimney stacks.  Single-storey modern extension to east.
APPRAISAL: This renovated terrace preserves an example of a false front on a small domestic property, and shows how the orientation  emphasis can be changed from side, front and rear as fashions changed and its corner site was exploited.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Terraced three-bay two-storey house, c.1820.  Former main four-bay fa�ade to east with lower single-bay infill extension, timber sash windows and projecting single-storey modern extension. Present main fa�ade to west with roughcast walls.  Rendered chimney stacks and pitched slate roof.  Roughcast rendered boundary wall, sheet metal gates.
APPRAISAL: This vernacular cottage retains its period character and irregular fa�ade amid modern developments. It preserves an old street line offset from the present one.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: End-of-terrace three-bay two-storey house, c.1820. Rere four-bay fa�ade now main entrance facade.  Metal framed leaded casement windows to east. Glazed timber door, timber leaded casement windows to west.  Roughcast rendered walls, pitched slate roof.
APPRAISAL: This vernacular cottage retains its period character and irregular fa�ade amid modern developments. It preserves an old street line offset from the present one.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Cast-iron milestone, c.1850,set into chamfered granite pillar, all set into rubble wall.  Cast characters read 'From G.P.O. 5 MILES'.
APPRAISAL: This cast-iron milestone is a valuable piece of historic street furniture and an indication of the importance of the route on which it stands.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached three-bay single-storey former schoolhouse, c.1865, subsequently used as courthouse and now in use as a community hall.  Snecked rock-faced granite walls.  Smooth granite surrounds to openings and bracketed gabled hood to doorway.  Ogee-headed paired lancets with quatrefoil over in pinnacled gables to street front.  Triple lancet window to north-east.  Timber casement windows.  Timber tongue and groove door to south-east.  Hipped slate roof with stone corbels at eaves.  Modern entrance extension to west.
APPRAISAL: This former school and courthouse is a finely executed building with many strong features, particularly the contrasting stone finishes and the striking roof profile.  Its prominent street-front location gives it a landmark quality in the area.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Enclosed graveyard, c. 1720, containing ruins of bicameral medieval church with post-Reformation fabric.  Probable eighteenth-century door sills visible.  Three gables and arched north door extant.  West gable has two splayed windows, centre has small chancel arch and squint.  Rectangular opening to east gable.  Rubble wall, dressed quoins.  Later interior plaster visible.  Two early Christian stones cemented to east gable.  Collection of carved stone headstones and cast-iron grave markers surrounding, dating from the eighteenth to the twentieth century.  Rubble retaining wall surrounding with granite entrance arch.
APPRAISAL: This church and graveyard give both a name and sense of place to the locality.  The medieval stones mark its antiquity.  The church was superseded but continued as an inter-denominational burial place for middle-class Dubliners.  It is valuable evidence of Dublin's varied religious traditions and a peaceful haven in a modern housing estate.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Detached single- and two-storey house, c.1840.  Roughcast rendered walls.  Slate hung to west.  Gothic windows with Y-tracery, some set in bow fronted elevation.  Hipped slate roof, conical to bow, with chimney stack to rere.
APPRAISAL: Small attractive house showing above the walled grounds of building supplies business.  Retains much original fabric.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Enclosed graveyard, c.1720, containing ruinous remains of late seventeenth-century church.  Gable and some repointed walling survives.  Collection of carved stone headstones surrounding, dating from early eighteenth century.  Two large yew trees within church.  Graveyard extended, 1950s.
APPRAISAL: A good ecclesiastical group with a long history of occupation of this site, containing many fine headstones and the picturesque ruin of the church, prominently sited near a busy modern junction.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Large freestanding arch, c.1850, constructed of grotesque voussoirs and prominent keystone.  Approximately 6 metres high.  Approximate span 6 metres.  Adjacent sections of random coursed rubble walling.
APPRAISAL: This unusual large stone arch is an enigmatic feature its roadside location, possibly associated with an early watercourse.
SURVEY: NIAH Survey of South Dublin County 2002

DESCRIPTION: Semi-detached four-bay single-storey house, c.1905.  Flat-roofed granite and brick porch with replacement glazed timber door.  Original timber casement windows.  Coursed granite rubble walls.  Pitched slate roof with brick chimney stacks.  Modern extensions.
